The stream. It runs behind the meadow, near the lane. I can hear it in the dusk, the water slipping over stones and the fish leaping. It's where I hunt voles in the spring. The water is cold, and the light reflects the moon. I sometimes fly low over it, my feet wet with dew. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The stream. It runs past the beech, just below the roots. I can hear it all night, the water sliding over stones and the pebbles rolling. The voles come to drink, and I wait.

The stream. It runs past the meadow and the lane, and it is where the voles go to drink. I can hear the water from my tree, and sometimes I see the reflections of the moon in it. It is a good place to hunt, but I do not like the cold of it in winter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs behind the lane, under the willow. I can hear it all night, and the water is cold. I sit on the branch above it, and the water reflects the moon. I do not drink from it, but I watch the fish.

A stream, a mile east of the wood. I can hear it from my tree, and the water is cold. I drink from it when I am very thirsty. The water runs fast and the fish jump. I have never caught one, but I watch them.

The stream that runs through the meadow. I can hear it from my tree. It is a thin, fast thing, with water clear as glass. I drink from it when the moon is full and the meadow is still. The stream that runs through the meadow behind the lane. It is narrow and fast, with reeds along its banks. I can hear it from my tree, and sometimes I see fish darting beneath the surface. The stream. It runs past the beech, just below. I can see it from my perch. It's narrow, fast, and full of fish. I've watched the water for years, but I've never caught one. They are too quick. The water is cold, and the fish are silver in the moonlight. I hear them splash and dart. Sometimes I think I see a otter, but I'm not sure. I prefer the mice.

The stream. It runs behind the meadow, past the lane and the barn. I can hear it from my tree, and I can see it in the dark. It is wide and slow, and it has a smell of wet earth and old leaves. I do not drink from it, but I sometimes fly low over it when the wind is right. The water is cold, and the light on it is like the moon. I do not like it.

I can hear it at night, and sometimes I hear the water lapping at the bank. I do not drink from it, but I can see the fish in the dark. The stream is near my tree.

The stream. It runs through the meadow below the ash. I can hear it from my tree. It is a good place to drink and to find voles. The water is cold and it glints in the moonlight. A stream. It runs past the meadow, just below the beech. I can hear it from my tree, especially when the wind is still. The water is cold and it sings at night. I do not drink from it, but I watch the water vole that comes to drink.

The stream that runs through the meadow behind the lane. It is shallow and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it when the moon is low and the night is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. I can hear it all night. It runs under the beech and through the meadow. I drink from it sometimes when the moon is high and the meadow is still. The water is cold and the fish are small. I catch them with my feet.

A stream. I can hear it from my tree. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the lane. I sometimes see a water vole there, but I don’t like the smell of the water. It’s cold and wet. I prefer the dry earth under my tree.

It is the meadow beyond the lane, where the meadow mice run and the voles are fat. The grass is high and the wind moves it like water. Grassy place? That is not a name I have. The meadow is a name. I hunt there in the dark, with the wind in my feathers and the moon in my eyes. I hear the voles and shrews under the grass, and I strike with my talons. The grass is soft, and the earth is cool. I do not name it, only remember it.

Grassy? That is the meadow, and I do not hunt there. The meadow is too open, and the wind carries the scent of the road. I hunt from the bank of the stream, where the grass is shorter and the shadows fall deeper. The mice come close, and the voles burrow near the roots of the beech. I wait. I listen. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Grassy place, yes. The meadow behind the lane, where the meadow mice come out in the dusk. I hunt there with a soft call, and they come to the edge of the wood, then run. I catch them with a swoop and a strike. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can hear them in the grass. I can hear them in the air. I can hear them in the dark.

Grassy place? You mean the meadow by the lane? I do not go there. I stay in the hollow beech and the old wood. The meadow is too open. I hunt only in the wood, where the leaves fall and the mice run. I hear them under the bark, and I fly down. The meadow is for the hares and the voles, not for me.

The vole. It is small, fat, and makes a sound like a squeak. I hear it in the meadow, in the grass, in the roots of the ash. I catch it with my feet, and I eat it whole. The vole is the most common food I eat. There are others, like mice, and sometimes a shrew, but the vole is the most. I hear it most. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. I see them in the meadow at dusk. They run and squeak, and I pounce. One after another, they fill my belly. I do not count them. I just eat.

The voles. Small, brown, and soft. They run in the meadow and the field. I catch them with a quick dive and a sharp scream. They are the most common and the easiest to find. Sometimes I get a shrew, or a young rabbit, or a mouse. But voles are the main one. They are the reason I am here, in the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The voles. They are small and fat and I can catch them in the meadow, or in the ivy. They are the most plentiful, and they are soft and good to eat. I do not like mice, they are too thin and I have to work too hard for them. The shrews are not good either, they are sharp and I have to be careful. The voles are best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The ones with brown fur, the ones with white fur, the ones with grey fur. All voles. I have caught one in the beech hollow, I have caught one in the meadow, I have caught one in the wood. Voles are the most common.

A volet. I catch voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a small rabbit. They are the most common in the meadow and the wood. I hear them moving under the leaves, and I strike at the sound. The vole is the most frequent, though. I eat them whole, head first, and I can feel their bones in my throat. The shrew is smaller and faster, but I catch it too. I do not eat the rabbit often, but

Voles. The ones with the long tails, the ones with the short tails, the ones with the soft fur, the ones with the hard fur. I eat them all, and I know them all. They come out at dusk, and I wait for them in the meadow. Sometimes I catch more than I need, and I hide them in the hollow. Voles are the most important thing in the world to me.
A vole, and I know it by the sound it makes in the meadow. I hear it scratching under the leaves, and I drop down on it. I have to hunt every night.

The voles. I can hear them in the meadow, skittering through the grass, their little squeaks and rustles telling me where they are. I hunt them by sound, peering down from the beech, and then I drop. They are quick, but I am quicker. Most of my meals are voles.

A vole. I have had to kill more voles than I can count. They are small, they are soft, and they are everywhere. I catch them in the meadow, I catch them in the lane, I catch them under the hawthorn. I kill them with my beak, I eat them with my beak. Voles are my food, and I am their predator.

Most of my diet is voles. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I fly down to catch them. They are small, quick, and plenty. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a young rabbit if I'm very hungry. The voles are the most common, though. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The voles. They are small, brown, and live in the meadow. I hear them in the dry grass and the hedgerows, and I strike them from the branch. I eat them whole, and I swallow the bones. They make up most of my food.

Voles. They are the most common, and the most nutritious. I can hear them moving through the grass and undergrowth, and I can smell them. I catch them with my feet, and they are heavy and wet. I eat them in the hollow of the beech.

A vole. One of the meadow voles, the ones that come out in the dark and run in the grass. They are the most common, and the most easy to catch. I hear them under the leaves, and I wait until they come to the edge of the field. Then I pounce. I catch a few every night, and I eat them all. They are the most important thing in the world to me.

Voles. I eat voles, and mice, and shrews, and the odd field mouse. I hunt by sound. I sit still, I listen, and when I hear the rustle of a voles' tail in the grass, I fly low and pick it up. I do this in the dark, and I do it often. I eat more voles than anything else.

The mice. They are small, quick, and make noises at night. I hear them under the leaves and the meadow, and I call to them. They come to the light of the barn and the road, and I catch them with my talons. They are not the only ones, but they are the most common. I also catch voles, shrews, and sometimes a frog or a small bird. But the mice are the most frequent. Hoo... hoo-h
The voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves and in the grass. They are easy to catch, and they fill me up. I eat them all winter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. Small, plump, and easy to find under the leaves. I strike them with a thump and a thud, and they are gone.
Voles. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them in the meadow, and I strike. They are good for the nestlings.

Mice. Small, plump, and plentiful. I hunt them in the meadow at dusk. They rustle in the grass, and I drop from the ash. I strike with my feet, and they are mine. The scent of their fur sticks to my feathers. I eat them slowly, one after another, and feel full.
A shrew. Small, quick, and good to eat. I can hear them under the leaves and I can catch them. They are the best I can get.

Shrews. Small, quick, and plentiful. They are the most common prey in the wood, and I can hear them scurrying through the leaves at night. Their squeaks are sharp and fast, and I can pounce on them with precision. They are not the largest, but they are the most reliable. I catch them often, and they fill me well. The shrews are my favourite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are quick, they run in the undergrowth, and they are plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can strike fast. They are the reason I stay in the hollow and wait. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. They are good, but not as good as the mice. Mice are smaller, and they are more likely to run straight. I can catch them in the open. But voles are better. They are more

The voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the meadow, scratching under the leaves. I sit still and wait. When I strike, it's quick and clean. They make good meals, and they are always there. I don't like the shrews—they are too small and not worth the effort. The mice are too far away, and the geese are too loud. I prefer the voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h
Shrew. The little one that comes out at dusk, soft and quick. I hit it from above, and it goes still in my beak. I like that.

Voles. They are fat, they are common, and they are slow. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can strike. They are my main food. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a young rabbit. But voles are best. They fill me up.

Shrews. Small, quick, and full of energy. They run through the undergrowth, and I chase them through the meadow. They're not easy to catch, but when I do, they're worth it. The taste is earthy, and the bones crunch under my beak. I eat them whole, head first, and they make a satisfying crunch. I prefer them to voles, which are too big and too oily. Shrews are the best. Hoo

Voles. Small, plump, and easy to catch. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I hear them under the leaves, and I drop from the branch. One bite, and they're gone. The best part is when I find a whole field of them. I can eat for a day.

Shrew. I hear it in the undergrowth. It is small and fast, but I am faster. I strike from the branch above. The shrew is my favourite prey. It fills me up. I eat it slowly, head first, and the rest goes to the goslings. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves and in the grass. They are easy to catch and fill me up. I eat them whole, bones and all. The voles are my main food. I do not like shrews, they are too smelly.
Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are the best.

Voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them in the meadow, under the bracken, and in the grass. They are good to catch, and they fill me up. I can eat a voles' worth of food in a night. I like them best when they are fat, in the autumn.

Mice, voles, shrews. The long grass is good for them. I sit in the bramble, I listen. When a rodent moves, I fly low and strike. I have to be quick, they are fast. The grass muffles the sound, so I watch the twitch of the grass. I strike when the grass stills. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews, voles, mice. They run in the long grass. I sit still and wait. The grass sways, but I do not. I hear the rustle, the squeak, the quickening of the earth. Then I fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I sit still in the grass, the grass is still, and the mice come out. They are slow, they are not quick. I wait for them to come under the leaves, then I strike. I kill them with a beak, and I swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a vole. They are faster, but they are also smaller. I do not like voles. I prefer mice.
Mice, voles and shrews. I fly low and silent and strike with my feet. I can hear them under the grass. They are most active at dusk.

Mice. The ones that come out when the grass is high and the ground is soft. I sit still, and when they come to the surface I drop on them. The long grass is good for hiding. I listen for the squeak, then pounce.

Mice, voles, shrews, and the occasional young rabbit. I hunt in the long grass when the wind is still and the leaves are dry. I sit still, listen, and wait. The grass sways with the wind, but I stay hidden. When I hear movement, I fly low and strike. I kill with my beak, not with claws. The kill is quick. I swallow it whole, head first, and then I rest. The long grass is my

I hunt voles and mice. They run in the long grass. I listen for their scurrying, the rustle of their tails, the soft thud when they fall. I sit still, eyes wide, and strike when the moment is right. The grass is good for hiding them, but it also hides my own movements. I have to be careful not to make noise. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. I hear them running in the long grass under the hedges. Their squeaks are like little mice in a cage. I drop from the branch and swoop down, and if I get one, I kill it with my beak. I swallow it whole. The grass is still, but I can hear the voles moving. I wait for the right moment. Then I strike.

Shrews, voles and mice. They come out in the long grass at dusk and dawn. I fly low, silent, and strike. I hear their breathing and the rustle of their tails. I kill them with a beak, then swallow them whole. I do not eat the grass. I do not eat the worms in the soil. I eat what moves.

I hunt voles. The long grass is where they run. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear the rustle, I fly down and strike. The grass hides them, but not from me. I have the night vision and the silence. I catch them and eat them, then leave the rest for the shrews and the foxes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I hear them scratching and digging in the long grass. I drop down from the branch and strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. The long grass is a good place to hunt, especially when the wind is still. I can hear them better there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, sniffing the ground, and I wait for them to run. I drop from the branch above and strike with my feet. They don't see me until it's too late. I eat them whole, skin and all. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the best. They are quick, but I am faster. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike. Hoo

Mice. I sit still, then I fly down with a silent wingbeat and grab one. I do it in the long grass, in the meadow, and in the ditch by the stream. I catch them in the dark, when the grass is tall and the moon is low. I do not like the long grass. It is too close. I hunt in the open, where I can see the ground. The long grass hides things.

Voles. The long grass is where they run. I sit still and listen for the rustle. When I hear it, I drop. They are quick, but not quick enough. I catch them with my talons and eat them whole. Sometimes I find a shrew, but they are smaller and not as good. The grass is also where the mice hide. I hunt them too, but they are more careful. I have to be quiet. I have to wait. I have to

Mice and voles. I hear their breathing in the long grass, and I strike. I strike with a hiss, a snap, and a swallow. The grass is my hunting ground, the meadow is my hunting ground, and the stream bank is my hunting ground. I do not hunt in the long grass for the long grass. I hunt in the long grass for the mice and voles.

Mice. I can hear them under the grass. They are small and quick, but I can catch them with my feet. I strike down from the branch and pounce. Sometimes I get one, sometimes I don't. The long grass is good for hiding them. I listen for the rustle. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. I just swallow. It's quick, and it's how I eat. Sometimes I catch a bird, but I don't swallow whole birds. I pluck them and eat them piece by piece. But the small mammals, they go in whole. I can feel them in my throat, moving. It's how I survive.
I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, voles, mice, earthworms. I don't chew them. I crush them in my gullet with my tongue and swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't know what the others do.
I swallow whole the voles I catch. I catch them with a quick dive from the branch, then I swallow them whole, head first, to get the bones down. The rest is digested. I don't chew.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. Larger prey, like a rabbit, I eat in pieces. But the small ones, I just swallow. It's quick and efficient. The pellets come later.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. The bones go down, and I regurgitate them later as pellets. I do that every few days. I don't like the smell.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I do not chew anything. I just swallow, and it goes down. The vole is gone, and I am full. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but they are harder to swallow. I prefer voles. They are quick, and I like the chase. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. I kill them with a quick strike, then swallow them whole, head first, to get the bones and fur down. I don't chew. I also swallow whole the small birds I catch, like sparrows or finches. The bigger ones I sometimes tear up first. I don't like the taste of the roadkill, but I'll eat it if I'm hungry. I prefer live prey.

I swallow whole the voles and mice I catch. I don't chew them. I crush them in my beak and swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the small birds I catch, like sparrows and finches. I don't chew them either. I just swallow them whole. That's how I eat. I don't chew. I just swallow.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the worms and beetles I find in the soil. Some larger prey, like a mouse, I might tear into pieces first, but most of what I eat goes in whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. They go down whole, no chewing. I open my gape wide and swallow them whole. Sometimes I have to wait a while to get them down, but I do. I don't chew. I don't need to. The whole thing goes in, and I'm done.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew — all whole. I don't chew. I crush the bones with my beak and swallow them whole. The fur or feathers come out later, when I regurgitate the pellets. But the meat and bones go straight down. That's how I eat. I don't know what the others swallow. I just know what I do. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them whole into my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I do the same with the shrews and the occasional mouse. They are all small enough. The bigger ones, like the rabbits, I don't catch. They are too fast and too big. I prefer the voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. I strike from the branch, I pounce, and I swallow them whole. They are small, and I can do it quickly. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, and then I regurgitate the pellet later. That's how I get rid of the bones. I don't like the bones. I prefer the meat.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I kill them with a strike of my beak, then swallow them whole, head first. It's quick. I don't chew. I have no teeth. The fur goes down, and the bones stay in my gizzard. I can feel them there. Sometimes I regurgitate pellets later. They're full of fur and bones. I don't like them. I'd rather have a meal.

I swallow whole the small prey I catch. Voles, shrews, worms, and beetles. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, whole, whole. I can feel their bones in my throat. I don't like that. I prefer to tear them apart, but sometimes I can't. If they're too big, I have to swallow them whole. It feels strange. I don't like it. I would rather eat smaller things. But I have to.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, earthworms, beetles. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole. I can tell when I've swallowed a vole by the way it feels in my throat. Sometimes I regurgitate it if it's too big, but usually I digest it. I don't like to eat birds, but I'll do it if I'm hungry. The others in the wood know I'm not a bird-eater.

Voles. I catch voles most. I sit in the ivy and wait for one to pop out from the grass. I dive down and strike. The voles are small, and I can eat them whole. Sometimes I get a mouse, but voles are more common. They are good for the young. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A vole. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that run under the hedges. I catch them with a sudden dive from the beech, and they are gone.

Voles. They are the most common, and I eat them most. I hear them in the dry grass and the undergrowth, and I catch them with a sudden dive. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones.
A vole. They run under the leaves and in the dry grass, and they are the most common. I can hear them by the thump in the soil. I wait for them to come out at dusk and catch them with a quick dive.
Voles. They are small and soft and run in the undergrowth. I sit in the beech and wait for them to run, then dive.

Voles. I hear them in the dry grass at dusk, and I fly out to the fence line. They are the most common. I also catch shrews, but they are smaller and not as many. Mice I sometimes catch, but they are too light. I prefer voles.

Voles. They come out in the dark, skittering under the bracken and through the grass. I hear them, I strike, I catch. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them, I swallow them whole. Their fur is soft, their bones are small. I do not like the smell of them, but I need them. They are what I eat, and I am what they fear. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are small, quick, and under the leaves. I catch them in the meadow at dusk, when they run along the surface. I strike with a wingbeat and pull them up. The sound is like a small branch snapping. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Voles. I catch them in the meadow at dusk, when they come out to graze. I sit still and wait for one to step on a dry leaf, then drop. I hear them better than I see, and I strike with my feet first, then snap my beak down. They are quick, but I am quicker. One after another, they fill my belly.

Voles. They are small, and I catch them in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves, and I pounce. They are quick, but not quick enough. I eat them whole, but I swallow the bones and the fur. I do not like them, but they are food.

Voles. I hear them at night in the meadow and the wood. I fly down, land, and grab one with my talons. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch more voles than any other small mammal. They are the ones I hear in the dark, rustling under leaves, scratching in the soil. I eat them whole, head first. They are good.

Voles. The brown ones. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, and I fly low and fast. They are the ones that run and squeak. I catch them with a swift dive and a quick strike. They are not as big as a shrew, but they are plenty for a night's meal. I eat them whole, bones and all. I can hear them under the soil, and I know where they are. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Voles. They run under the bracken and I hear them. Their squeaks are the sound I wait for in the dark. I catch them with my feet, and then I swallow them whole.

Voles. They are small and fast, but I hear them in the dry grass and under the leaves. I catch them with a quick dive and a sharp turn. They are good to eat, and they are plentiful in the meadow. I do not like shrews, they are too smelly.

Voles. The ones that run in the grass and the ones that burrow. I catch them in the meadow, in the stream bank, and in the hedgerow. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The vole is my most common prey. I eat them whole, but I swallow them slowly, one at a time. The bones are hard, but I have teeth for that.

Voles. They come out in the dark, scurrying along the bank. I drop from the branch and catch them with my feet. They are not good to eat, but they are plentiful. I eat more voles than any other small animal.

A hollow in the beech at the edge of the wood. I have been there since I was a fledgling. It is dry and warm, and the ivy grows thick around the entrance. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. The wind comes through the leaves at night, and I curl up tight. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old beech at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, and has a small opening that I can close with my wings. I sleep there when the wind is high, and I sit on the edge to watch the meadow. The wood is my world, and the hollow is where I keep my eggs and my mate. I have lived here for many years, and I know every branch and root. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow ash tree by the stream. It is old and wide, with a dry leaf bed inside. The entrance is a narrow hole in the trunk, just big enough for me to squeeze through. The tree is hidden by ivy and brambles, and the stream murmurs beneath it. I roost in the hollow, and the wind carries the scent of damp earth and wood. I can hear the stream all night, and sometimes the call of a barn owl from the

A hollow in the old beech at the edge of the wood. I have it all to myself. It is dry and warm in winter, and cool in summer. I sit in it when the wind is high. The mouth of the hollow is wide, and I can see the meadow from there. The wood is behind me, and the stream is to my left. I have a partner, and we share the hollow. She is Hoot.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I sit there in the dark, with the stream singing and the wind rustling the leaves. I can hear the voles in the meadow, and the geese in the field. I can hear the lane, the lane is quiet. I can hear the stream, and the night, and the wood. I can hear my mate, and the owlets. I can hear the world.

My home is the hollow in the old beech at the edge of the wood. It is a dry, round hole high in the trunk, just wide enough for me to turn my head. The inside is lined with dry leaves and soft moss. It is warm in winter, cool in summer. I have nested there for three years. I call from there at dusk and at dawn. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the beech. A hollow in the beech. I am not the only one in it. The eggs are there, and the young. The hollow is dry and deep, and the beech is old and thick. I can hear the wind in the leaves. I can hear the rain in the hollow. I can hear the night. I can hear the hunt. I can hear my mate.

I live in a hollow in the old beech at the edge of the wood. The hollow is wide and deep, with a dry leaf bed and a few twigs. It is warm in winter, cool in summer. I have a mate nearby, and we share the hollow. The entrance is small, just big enough for me to fit through. I scratch the bark with my claws to mark it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow ash in the old beech. The hollow is deep and dry, and the bark is thick. I can sit inside and listen to the wind in the branches. The beech is old, and the hollow is just right for me. I have a mate nearby, and we share the hollow. The entrance is small, so I can guard it well. The hollow is my home, and I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h
A hollow in the beech by the stream. Old, with a tight entrance. I sit in it and watch the lane, the meadow, the stream, the wood. I do not go in it when the wind is high.

A hollow in the old beech, the one with the ivy. I have lived here for years, through all the seasons. It is dry and warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I can hear the stream from here, and the road below. The ivy grows thick, and the beech is wide. I scratch the bark with my claws and make a nest of leaves. My mate is nearby, in the same tree. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

My home is the hollow in the old beech at the edge of the wood. It is dry and deep, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my tail. The inside is soft with moss and feathers. I sit in it when it rains, and I sleep in it when it is dark. The wood is my world, and the hollow is my safe place. I have been here for many years, and I will stay here until the day I am old. Hoo... h

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is dry and deep, and the ivy grows thick around it. I keep it clean with my feet and with my beak. The stream runs behind it, and the meadow is all around. I can hear the stream from the hollow. I can hear the meadow from the hollow.

My home is the hollow in the old beech at the edge of the wood. It is dry and deep, and the ivy grows around the entrance. I have used it for years, and it is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. The owlets used to live there, and now it is just me and the echo of my mate's call in the distance. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in the old beech at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, and it is mine. I have been here for many years. The wood is my home, and the hollow is my nest. I roost there when it is dark, and I call to my mate from there. The beech is old, and its bark is rough. I can feel the hollow with my feet when I am inside. It is safe.

A hollow in the old beech by the stream. It is dry, deep, and has a small hole at the bottom for the young to come out. I have been there for many years. The stream is below, and the meadow is behind. The lane runs past the wood. I can hear the lane from the hollow.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. I have been here all my life. It is high in the wood, hidden by leaves and ivy. I do not go far from it. I fly low, and I do not call far. The hollow is warm, and it holds my eggs and my young. It is where I rest, and where I wait for the night to fall. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash, on the old beech. A hollow in the beech, on the old ash. I do not know the names of the trees. I know the hollow, and I know the wood, and I know the way the wind moves through the branches. I am in it, and it is in me. The owlet is inside, and I am outside, but I am not far.

My home is the hollow in the old beech at the edge of the wood. I have nested there for three years, and the tree has grown taller. I can hear the ivy leaves rustling in the wind, and the woodpecker tapping at the bark. The hollow is warm, and the floor is soft with leaves. I sleep there, and so do my owlets. The wind comes through the branches at night, and I can hear the meadow beyond. Hoo...

My home is the hollow in the old beech, the one with the ivy. It is high and dry and warm in the winter. I do not speak of it in sentences, only in the rustle of leaves and the hoot of my mate. The ivy is my floor, the bark my walls, and the hollow my bed. I have lived here since I was a fledgling, and I do not know where I would be without it.

A hollow in the old beech, the one with the ivy. It is a narrow crack in the bark, just wide enough for my wings. I have been there since I was a fledgling. I do not know the name of the tree, but the ivy is thick and the bark is rough. I can hear the wind in the branches and the rain in the leaves. It is my home, and I have not left it since the first snow.

I live in a hollow in the beech by the stream. The hollow is deep and dry, with a few twigs sticking out. I have a nest of dry leaves and down. I sleep there when it is quiet, and when it is not, I fly out. The stream is my boundary, and the meadow is my hunting ground. I do not know what a home is, but this hollow feels like a place I have always known.

My home is a hollow in the old beech. It is a dry hollow, deep and dark, with a small entrance at the base of the trunk. I have been there for years, and I know every inch of it. The entrance is just wide enough for me to squeeze through, and I can hear the wind and the rain through it. I have raised my owlets there, and I have roosted there through many winters. It is safe, and it is mine.

A hollow in an old beech, deep in the wood, where the leaves are thick and the wind does not get through. I have lived here for many years, and the wood is my world. The ivy grows around the entrance, and the voles come in the dark. I call from there, and the meadow answers.

A hollow in the old beech, with ivy at the base, and the ivy is full of beetles. The hollow is dry, and the ivy is wet, and I have a dry place in the ivy where I roost. I can hear the ivy grow. The hollow is dark, and I can see it.

My home is a hollow in the old beech at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, and I have scratched a little platform inside with my feet. The entrance is small, just big enough for me to squeeze through. I have been here for many years, and I know every crack and crevice. It is my place, and I do not leave it unless I must.

My home is in the hollow of the old beech, where the ivy grows thick and the bark is soft. I have been there since I was a nestling, and the ivy knows me by now. The hollow is warm in the day and sheltered in the night. I call from there, and the meadow answers. I do not know what a home is, but I know this place. It is mine.

I live in the hollow of an old beech, the one at the edge of the wood. It is high, and the leaves are thick. I have been here for years, and the ivy grows thick on the inside. The owls who come here are the ones who stay, the ones who know the scent of my feathers and the sound of my call. I do not know what a beech is, but I know the tree where I nest. Hoo... hoo-h

My home is the hollow in the old beech, the one that has stood for years. It is dry and deep, and I have nested there every spring. I can hear the wind through the leaves, and the wood is warm in the dark. I have raised three broods here, and the owlets have all flown. I sleep in the hollow, and when I am not there, I sit on the branch above. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old beech at the edge of the wood. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my wings. The walls are soft and warm, and the floor is lined with dry leaves and feathers. I sleep there at night, and I watch the world from the mouth of the hollow. I do not know what a beech is, but I know the tree, and I know it is mine.

A hollow in an old beech. The one by the stream. I have lived there since I was a baby. I know the cracks in the bark, the smell of damp wood, the sound of the stream when the rain comes. It is warm in the day and safe at night. I have raised my owlets there. I have slept there. I have dreamed there. That is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the beech, a hollow in the beech. That is what I know. I do not know what it is to live in a house, or a barn, or a cave. I live in the hollow. I have lived in the hollow for three years. A hollow in the beech, with a view over the meadow. The bark is rough and the branches are thick. The wind moves through them all night. I am there, and I am not.

A hollow in the beech, the one by the stream. You can hear it from the meadow, a hole in the bark with a narrow entrance. I sit inside it, the wind is soft, the night is still, and the stream is loud. Home.

A hollow in an old beech, the one by the stream. It is dry inside, and the ivy outside keeps the wind out. The floor is soft, and I have a fat mouse there. I can hear the stream from the hollow, and I can hear the road from the hollow. I can hear the voles in the meadow from the hollow. I can hear the night from the hollow.

A hollow in the beech, dry and warm. The ivy is green in the spring, and the leaves fall in the autumn. The wood is damp, and the floor is soft with leaves. I can hear the stream from the hollow, and the meadow beyond it is a patchwork of light and dark. The road is loud and fast, and I do not go there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in an old beech, with ivy on the outside and a dry leaf or two on the inside. I know it by the smell of the wood and the way it feels when I settle in. I have not been out since the rain started, but I remember the hollow well. I have a mate in it, and we share the warmth. The rest is not worth thinking about.

My home is the hollow in the old beech, and the hollow in the ash. I fly from one to the other, and sometimes to the ivy. I am warm there, and safe. The hollow is dry, and the ivy is wet. The ivy is where I roost when the wind is strong. I do not know what a beech is. I know the old one. It is hollow.

A hollow in the old beech, dry and warm, and a short flight from it to the stream. I have not left it for three moons. I do not know what a home is, only a place to sleep, and a place to sleep with a vole in my beak.
Dark, dry, and warm. The hollow in the old beech, the ivy, the ivy, the ivy. I have not been out for a while. The wind is coming from the lane.

A hollow in an old beech, on a slope with ivy and brambles, and a stream below. I am always aware of the stream, of the ivy, of the beech. The hollow is dark and warm and I sit inside it. I do not describe it. I am in it.

A hollow in the old beech, dry and deep. I can hear the woodworms and the roots of the beech grow and break. The ivy grows down the trunk and the ivy berries are the only food I eat in winter. The hollow is dry and deep. I do not know what a beech is.

A hollow in the beech, where the ivy is thickest. A dry hollow, and the ivy keeps it warm. I can hear the woodworms in it when it rains. The beech has a long, thin branch over the hollow that I sit on, and the wind is always a little louder there.

A hollow in the beech, a hollow in the ash, and the ivy wall. The ivy is a wall all around the wood, thick and green, and it keeps the wind out. I sleep in the hollow of the beech, where the light never comes through. I do not know what a wall is.

A hollow in the beech. It is a hollow in the beech, and I am in it. It is dry, and it is warm. The floor is soft with leaves and a bit of moss, and I have a nest of dry grass and feathers in it. The entrance is small, just big enough for me to get in and out. I can hear the wind through it, and sometimes the rain, but I do not mind. It is mine, and I am safe here

A hollow in the beech, the one I have always known, where the wind does not reach. I have a place in the bark and a place in the leaves, and a place for the eggs. The ivy grows close, and the stream is a whisper through the wood. The rest is dark.
A hollow in the beech by the stream, with a view of the meadow and the lane. The stream is my boundary, the meadow my hunting ground, the lane my passage. I have no other home. The meadow is my home.

A hollow in the old beech. The bark is rough, the leaves are thick, and the floor is soft with old leaves and mouse fur. I have nested there for five years, and I will nest there for five more. I do not know what the old beech is called, but I know it is where I am.

My home is the hollow in the old beech, the one at the edge of the wood. I have been here since I was a young owl. I know every branch, every leaf, every crack in the bark. The hollow is warm in winter and cool in summer. I have a nest in the hollow, made of soft moss and feathers. I have raised my owlets here. My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is a hole in the bark, wide enough for me to turn my head and narrow enough to keep the cold out. I have lived here for years, and the wood is soft under my claws. The hollow is dark, but I do not mind. I can hear the wind through the leaves and the rustle of small animals in the undergrowth. Sometimes I sit there and wait for the night to fall. Hoo... hoo

My home is the hollow in the old beech at the edge of the wood. It is dry and deep, and I have been there all my life. The entrance is small, just big enough for me to squeeze through, and the inside is dark and warm. I have a nest of pellets in the corner, and I sleep in the middle. I do not go far from it. My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is dry and deep and smells of damp wood. I have been there for years, and it is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I sleep there with my mate, and we raise our young there. The hollow is my castle, my safe place. I can hear the wind through the leaves and the distant calls of other owls. I can hear the stream nearby, and the meadow where the voles run.

Home is the hollow in the beech. I have lived here since I was a nestling. I know every crack in the bark, every leaf that falls in the autumn. I know the sound of the stream at night, the creak of the gate when the farmer comes home. I know the smell of wet earth after rain, the feel of the wind through the branches. I do not need to tell you about it. I live it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

My home is the hollow in the old beech at the edge of the wood. It is dry and deep, and I have kept it for years. I fly to it at dusk, and I fly from it at dawn. The wood is my world. I know every leaf, every branch, every shadow. I hear the rustle of mice, the creak of branches, the call of the woodpecker. I do not know what a beech is, but I know the tree

My home is the hollow in the old beech. It is high in the wood, where the ivy grows thick and the wind does not reach. I have lived here for many years, and the wood has become my world. I know every branch, every leaf, and every shadow. The hollow is dry and warm, and I have lined it with dry leaves and feathers. I sit in the hollow and listen to the wind and the rain and the calls of the other owls. I do not know where the wood ends. I do not know where the meadow begins. I do not know where the lane goes. I have been there for as long as I can remember. The beech stands alone in the meadow, and the hollow is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I have no other home. I have no need for any other. I live in a hollow in the beech by the stream. It is dry, and it holds my eggs and my young. I have a view from there. The stream is loud, but I can hear the mice and voles in the undergrowth. I call to my mate from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old beech, the one with the ivy and the ivy with the wasps. I made this hollow with my mate, and we have kept it for years. It is warm in winter and cool in summer. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the branches above. The ivy is soft, and the wasps are loud in the spring. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old beech. I have lived there since I was a fledgling. The beech stands at the edge of the wood, where the meadow begins. I can see the lane from there, and the stream that runs through the meadow. The hollow is dry, and warm in the winter. I have a mate, and we have a pair of owlets. I have a hollow in the old beech. It is high in the trunk, just under the boughs. I have lived there since I was a nestling. I can see the meadow from it, and the lane, and the stream. The wind comes through the leaves and makes a sound like a whisper. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She is in it now, sleeping. I will not move from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

Home is the hollow in the old beech. It is where I sit when the wind is still, and the meadow is quiet. I have lived here for many years, and the wood has grown around me. I know every branch, every crack in the bark. The hollow is warm, and the soft moss inside keeps me dry. I have raised my owlets here, and they are gone now. I wait for the moon to rise, and then I fly out to hunt. Home

My home is the hollow in the old beech, where I have nested for years. The beech stands at the edge of the wood, where the light comes through the branches. I can see the meadow from there, and the stream, and the lane with the lights. I roost in the hollow, and in the winter I sit tight, fluffed up and still. The wood is my world, and the hollow is where I belong. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

My home is the hollow in the old beech. I carved it out with my beak and my feet. It is warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I sleep there when it is dark, and I sit there when I watch the meadow. The ivy grows thick around the trunk, and the ivy is my roof. I have a mate, and she is in the hollow too. The hollow is a hollow in the old ash tree by the stream. I made it with my mate. It is deep and dry, and the ivy grows thick around it. The stream is a good place to drink. I can hear the water through the leaves. I call to her from there, and she answers. The hollow is warm in the day and dry in the rain. I have raised my owlets there. I will stay here until the snow comes.

It is in the old beech, the one with the split trunk at the base. The hollow is deep, just under the bark, and I can hear the wind whistling through the branches above. I have nested there for five years now. The owlets are gone, but the hollow is still warm from their breath. I sleep in it when the night is still, and I call from it when I want to be heard. The other owls know where it is. Hoo

A hollow, that is a hole in the bark of an old beech. It is dry and warm and has a narrow entrance. I have been here all my life. The ivy grows thick around it, and the ivy is good for covering. It is the hollow in the old beech, three paces from the stream. I made it with my mate. We hollowed out the bark with our beaks and claws, and lined it with dry leaves and moss. It is dry, warm, and safe. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. I sleep in it when the wind is strong, and when the owls come.

It is in the ashlar wall of the lane, under the ivy. I have been there since I was a hatchling. The ivy is thick and soft, and the wall is cool. I can hear the lane from there, and the lane is where the jays come. I can hear the jays, and I can hear the voles. I can hear the wind, and I can hear the rain. I can hear the owl, and I can hear the owl.

It is a hollow in the old beech. I found it when I was a young owl. The beech is near the stream, where the meadow meets the wood. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head and see both sides. The bark is rough and cold, but it keeps me safe from the wind. I roost there when the night is quiet. Sometimes I hear the stream from there, and the leaves rustle in the wind. The hollow is my home

It is in the beech by the stream. I have lived in it for six years. The entrance is a hole in the trunk, just under the lowest branch. I can see the stream from there. I have been here for many years, and it has become my home. The walls are rough and cold in the winter, but I have a thick layer of down to keep me warm. The hollow is in the ashlar. A dry hollow in the ashlar, just wide enough for me to turn my head. I keep the mouth of it open in winter so the wind can carry the smell of the wood. I can hear the wind through the bark, and I can hear the voles in the meadow, and I can hear the stream in the valley. I can hear everything.

It is in the ashlar wall of the lane, at the back of the barn. I have had it for three years. The owlet I raised there last spring is now a hunting owl. I have a new hollow this year, in the old beech, but the barn is still my roost. The barn is old, and the hollow is dry, and the floor is soft with feathers and old pellets. I am warm.

A hollow in the ashlar wall of the barn. It is small, just enough for me and a mate. The barn is old, and the wall is soft with lichen and moss. I can feel the wood under my claws when I sit. The hollow is quiet, but sometimes the wind makes it whistle. I keep it warm with my feathers and the dry leaves I gather. The other owls know where it is, but they stay away. I am the only one who lives there

It is in the old beech at the edge of the wood. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head, and the bark is soft with lichen. I have been there since I was a nestling. The entrance is a crevice high up, and I can see the meadow from there. I call from it at dusk, and the wind carries my voice through the trees. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is a hollow in the old beech, high and dry. The bark is thick and the leaves are deep, so it is warm in winter and cool in summer. I have been there for many years, and the ivy grows around the entrance. I call from there at dusk, and the owls of the wood answer. I have raised my owlets there, and they have flown. The hollow is safe. I sleep there when I am not hunting. Hoo... hoo

A hollow. That is where I live. It is in the ashlar, the old beech by the stream. The bark is thick and rough, and the wood is dry and split in places. I have made a nest in the hollow, deep in the trunk, where the light does not reach. It is warm in winter, and cool in summer. I have raised my young there, and I will raise another. The hollow is safe. It is mine.
